issue.issue_text: Whether the plea of implied repeal is valid.

facts: The case involved a prosecution for the sale of adulterated vinegar under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (Adulteration Act).
The defense argued that the Adulteration Act was impliedly repealed by a later law, the Fruit Products Order, 1955 (Fruit Order), and therefore the prosecution was not valid.
law: The Court established the general principles for implied repeal, stating that courts lean against it.
A later law is presumed to repeal an earlier one only when the two are so inconsistent or repugnant that they cannot stand together.
For an implied repeal to be valid, the two provisions must be wholly incompatible, and their simultaneous operation must lead to absurd consequences.
If the objects of the two statutes are different and each is restricted to its own subject, they are generally intended to run in parallel without conflict, even if there is an apparent overlap.
An implied repeal is only sustained when a consistent body of law cannot be maintained without abrogating the previous law.
application: The Court scrutinized both the Adulteration Act and the Fruit Order to determine if they were irreconcilably in conflict.
It found that the party arguing for repeal failed to show any "fatal conflict or inconsistency" between the two laws with respect to the specific charges of selling adulterated vinegar.
The Court concluded that the two statutory provisions could operate harmoniously within their respective spheres without causing confusion or absurd results.
It determined that the scheme of the Adulteration Act could easily fit within the scheme of the Fruit Order, suggesting they could coexist.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the plea of implied repeal, holding that the Fruit Products Order did not repeal the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act because the two laws were not so repugnant that they could not stand together and could operate harmoniously.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the plea of implied repeal is valid.
appellant_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the appellant's arguments, but their position, which the court accepted, was that the plea of implied repeal must fail.
respondent_arguments: There is an irreconcilable conflict between the two statutory provisions (the Fruit Order and the Adulteration Act).

The Fruit Order is not only later in date but also has an overriding effect over all other laws by virtue of s. 3(6) of the Essential Commodities Act, and therefore must prevail over the Adulteration Act.

Under the Fruit Order, prosecution can only be initiated with the prior sanction of the Licensing Officer, whereas under the Adulteration Act, even a purchaser can initiate prosecution without such sanction.
Unlike the Fruit Order, the Adulteration Act (in s. 20-A) empowers the court to implead the manufacturer, distributor, or dealer.

cases.principle: When two Acts are inconsistent or repugnant the later will be read as having impliedly repealed the earlier.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A later statute impliedly repeals an earlier one only when the two provisions are so plainly repugnant and wholly incompatible that they cannot stand together, making it impossible on any reasonable hypothesis to give effect to both. If the objects of the two statutes are different and the language of each is restricted to its own subject, they are generally intended to run in parallel without real conflict, and no implied repeal will be found.
obiter: The legislature is presumed to intend to enact a consistent and harmonious body of laws and is not expected to create confusion by omitting an express repeal.
Statutes that are in pari materia, even if in apparent conflict, should be construed to be in harmony with each other as far as reasonably possible.
Where an act or omission constitutes an offence under two or more enactments, the offender is liable to be prosecuted under either but shall not be punished twice for the same offence.
The rule of irreconcilable repugnancy also controls the implied repeal of a general statute by a special statute.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The provisions of the Adulteration Act and the Fruit Order serve different purposes and are supplementary, not contradictory. The Adulteration Act is concerned with public health, while the Fruit Order aims for the equitable distribution of essential commodities. As such, they can operate in parallel without conflict, and the plea of implied repeal must be rejected.
legal_tests_applied: The courts, as a rule, lean against implying a repeal unless the two provisions are so plainly repugnant to each other that they cannot stand together and it is not possible on any reasonable hypothesis to give effect to both at the same time.

The repeal must, if not express, flow from necessary implication as the only intendment. The provisions must be wholly incompatible with each other so that the two provisions operating together would lead to absurd consequences, which intention could not reasonably be imputed to the legislature.

To determine if a later statutory provision repeals by implication an earlier one it is accordingly necessary to closely scrutinise and consider the true meaning and effect both of the earlier and the later statute. If the objects of the two statutory provisions are different and the language of each statute is restricted to its own object or subject, then they are generally intended to run in parallel lines without meeting and there would be no real conflict.
why_respondent_won: The two statutes have different objects and can operate in parallel without conflict; the Adulteration Act concerns public health while the Fruit Order concerns the equitable distribution of essential commodities. The court stated: 'If the objects of the two statutory provisions are different and the language of each statute is restricted to its own objects or subject, then they are generally intended to run in parallel lines without meeting and there would be no real conflict'.

The provisions of the two statutes are supplementary and cumulative, not irreconcilably conflicting. The court found: 'our attention was not drawn to any provision of the Adulteration Act and Rules, compliance with which would result in breach of any mandate, whether affirmative or negative; of the Fruit Order.'

The statutes can function together without creating absurd consequences or fatal inconsistencies. The court noted: 'Both the statutes can function with full vigour side by side in their own parallel channels.'

Even in cases of overlap, there is a safeguard against double punishment. The court pointed out: 'Even if they happen to some extent to overlap, s. 26 of the General Clauses Act fully protects the guilty parties against double jeopardy or double penalty.'
policy_considerations: As the legislature must be presumed in deference to the rule of law to intend to enact consistent and harmonious body of laws, a subsequent legislation may not be too readily presumed to effectuate a repeal of existing statutory laws in the absence of express or at least clear and unambiguous indication to that effect. This is essential in the interest of certainty and consistency in the laws which the citizens are enjoined and expected to obey.
